course_description:
This course introduces students to the process of designing a research project, focusing in particular on common approaches to data collection and analysis in social science research. Students will develop an understanding of the relative merits of contrasting methodologies, and skills in identifying methodological rigour and ethical design.

In this course, students will learn to develop research questions, locate them within a theoretical framework, identify the most appropriate methodological designs and methods to answer them, and consider the ethical implications of their research. At the end of the course, students should be able to develop a research project suitable for Masters level. Even if you are not planning to undertake a thesis, these exercises will enhance your critical skills as a consumer of social research, thus delivering benefits for your current studies and beyond.

course_aims: The main aim of this course is to introduce students to the research process in the social sciences, including how to choose research questions and undertake a literature review, as well as introduce students to a range of methods and methodologies commonly used. This course will assist students in designing a viable research proposal appropriate for a Masters level project. By the end of the course students should have developed a sophisticated understanding of the research process, the relative merits of contrasting methodological approaches to social inquiry and an appreciation of the issues that need to be considered in order to produce ethically sound social research.

learning_outcomes.description: Demonstrate a well-founded knowledge of the key ideas and issues in the field of research methods.
Demonstrate acquired conceptual and analytical capacities, along with an ability to apply these skills as appropriate.
Develop intellectual tools and skills that will make you more competitive in your future professional activities in a variety of fields and positions.

learning_activities.topic: Week 1 – What is research design for? Questions, claims, and contribution This week introduces the course and considers what research design is for in graduate study. Students will examine how research questions, claims, and contributions are formed, and why they matter for building a viable project. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 2 – Research problems, puzzles, and the shaping of a question This week focuses on how broad interests are turned into researchable problems and puzzles. Students will work on refining research questions so they are clear, focused, and feasible. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 3 – Literature reviews, concepts, and positioning a project This week examines how literature reviews help locate a project within existing scholarship. Students will consider how concepts are defined and how a project can be positioned in relation to relevant debates Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 4 – Document analysis, corpus selection and coding logic This week introduces documents as a source of evidence in social research. Students will consider how to select a document corpus and how qualitative coding can be used to organise and interpret documentary material. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 5 – Introduction to qualitative coding This week provides an introduction to the logic and practice of qualitative coding. Students will work with sample materials to identify themes, categories, and patterns in a systematic way. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Week 6 – Course Reading Week No seminar this week. Students are expected to use this time to consolidate course readings and prepare for the second half of semester.

Week 7 – Online lecture: Qualitative research design: interviews, observation, documents, fieldwork This pre-recorded online lecture introduces key approaches to qualitative research design. It considers how different forms of qualitative evidence are generated and the kinds of claims they can support. There will be no in person class this week. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 8 – Interviews and field notes This week focuses on interviews as a method of data collection and on the role of field notes in qualitative research. Students will consider how interview design, note-taking, and reflection shape the quality of research evidence. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 9 – Ethics, power, positionality, and risk This week examines ethical issues in research design, including informed consent, confidentiality, harm, and researcher responsibility. It also considers how power, positionality, and risk shape the conduct of research. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 10 – Quantitative reasoning for non-specialists This week introduces quantitative reasoning for students who are not specialising in quantitative methods. It focuses on how to read, interpret, and critically assess quantitative evidence in social research. This week will be a make-up class sometime during the week because of the public holiday. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 11 – Case studies, historical analysis and process tracing This week explores case study research and within-case analysis. Students will be introduced to historical analysis and process tracing as ways of explaining political and social outcomes. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 12 – Mixed methods, triangulation, and combining forms of evidence This week considers how qualitative and quantitative approaches can be combined in a single research design. Students will examine triangulation and the strengths and limitations of mixed methods research. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 13 – Conclusion: AI and research practice This final week reflects on the role of AI and digital tools in contemporary research practice. It also reviews the course as a whole and considers how students can apply its lessons to their own research projects. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
